title: Multiple Choice & Matching
summary: Four question families sit under one roof here: multiple choice, matching information to paragraphs, matching features to a list, and matching sentence endings. They share one enemy — the plausible wrong answer built from words lifted straight out of the passage. This lesson shows you how to beat it.

seo.title: IELTS Reading: Multiple Choice & Matching | GrowQR
seo.description: IELTS multiple choice and matching questions explained — paragraph matching, features and sentence endings. Beat distractors and pick the right answer.

objectives: Answer multiple-choice questions by paraphrase-matching and eliminating distractors
Locate the right paragraph in Matching Information without reading in order
Match statements to a reusable list of features without over-relying on repeated words
Use grammar and meaning together to complete Matching Sentence Endings

blocks.html:
Multiple choice and matching questions look friendly. The answer is right there in front of you — you just pick it. That is exactly why candidates lose marks on them. The examiner isn't testing whether you can find words; they're testing whether you can tell the difference between what the passage actually says and what merely sounds like it. Every one of these question types is built around a small number of near-misses, and the whole game is refusing to be fooled by them.

These types appear in both Academic and General Training Reading — the texts differ, the questions do not. Get comfortable with the four families below and you've covered a large slice of the forty marks.

1. Multiple choice

You'll meet two shapes. The common one gives a stem and four options (A–D); you choose one. The less common one gives a longer list — say seven options — and asks you to choose two or three, each worth its own mark. Read the instruction line every time, because circling one answer when the task wants two throws away marks you'd otherwise have earned.

The correct option is almost never a copy of the passage's wording. It's a paraphrase: same idea, different words. Meanwhile the wrong options often do reuse the passage's exact vocabulary — which is the trap. Your eye jumps to the familiar phrase and picks it, even though the sentence around it says something different, or something the passage never claimed.

blocks.title: A reliable method for multiple choice
items: Read the stem first, ignore the options. Turn the question into your own words so you know what you're hunting for before the options can bias you.
Locate the relevant lines in the passage. The questions follow the order of the text, so the answer to Q3 sits after Q2's and before Q4's — use that to narrow your search.
Answer from the passage, then match to an option. Decide what the text says, then find the option that paraphrases it — don't shop the options against the passage one by one.
Eliminate, don't just select. Cross out each wrong option and know why it's wrong: too extreme, not mentioned, or true-but-not-the-answer.
Check the whole option is right. An option can be half-correct — the first clause matches the passage, the second doesn't. Half right is wrong.

blocks.title: The three distractor traps
blocks.html: Wrong options are engineered, not random. Watch for: (1) Word-match traps — the option reuses a memorable word from the passage but changes the claim. (2) Overstatement — the passage says "some researchers suggest", the option says "researchers have proven"; words like all, always, only, never are red flags. (3) True but irrelevant — the option is a true statement from elsewhere in the text, just not the answer to this stem.

blocks.title: Multiple choice in action
blocks.prompt:
Passage extract: "When the town's public library switched to Sunday opening in 2019, staff braced for complaints about the extra cost. Instead, weekend visits climbed by nearly a third within a year, and the borrowing figures that had drifted downwards for a decade steadied. Managers were quick to credit the new hours, though a redesigned children's section had opened the same spring."

Question: What does the passage suggest about the rise in weekend visits?

A. It was entirely caused by the new Sunday hours.
B. It reversed a long decline in borrowing overnight.
C. It may not be due to the new hours alone.
D. It led to complaints about the extra cost.
blocks.explain: The final sentence is the key: managers credit the hours, "though" a new children's section opened at the same time — the passage deliberately flags a second possible cause, so the rise can't be pinned on Sunday opening alone. A overstates with "entirely". B misreads the text: borrowing steadied, it wasn't reversed, and "overnight" is invented. D is a word-match trap — "complaints" and "extra cost" appear in the passage, but as something staff expected, not something that happened.

blocks.html:
2. Matching Information (which paragraph?)

You're given a set of statements — a specific fact, an example, a reason, a comparison — and you must say which lettered paragraph contains each one. Two things make this type distinctive, and both are stated in the instructions:

  • The answers are not in passage order. A statement about paragraph F may come before one about paragraph B. This is the one major type where you cannot use sequence to help you.
  • A paragraph may be used more than once, or not at all. Don't assume every paragraph gets exactly one answer, and don't cross a paragraph off just because you've already used it.

Because you're hunting for a specific detail, not the main idea, this is a scanning task, not a skimming one. Focus on the concrete signal in each statement — a name, a number, a process, an example — and scan the paragraphs for that.

blocks.title: Matching Information vs Matching Headings
blocks.html: Don't confuse the two. Matching Headings asks for the main idea of each paragraph and every paragraph gets one heading. Matching Information asks which paragraph contains a specific detail, paragraphs can repeat or go unused, and the answers aren't in order. Read the instruction line so you know which game you're playing.

3. Matching Features

Here you match a list of statements to a list of options — often researchers, people, places, years, or categories. For example, five findings must each be matched to the scientist who made them. As with Matching Information, an option can be used more than once unless the instructions say otherwise, and there may be more options than you need.

The obvious tactic — find the name, read the sentence next to it — works, but it's also where the traps live. A passage discussing three researchers will often mention one researcher's view inside the sentence about another ("Unlike Patel, Osei argued that…"). Match the claim to the right person, not just the nearest name.

blocks.title: Working through Matching Features
items: Underline every option in the passage first. Names and years are capitalised or numeric, so they jump off the page — mark them all before you start matching.
Read the full sentence around each mention, not just the clause touching the name. Attribution can sit a line away from the name itself.
Match by meaning, then confirm the person. Two researchers may hold similar-sounding views; the deciding detail is usually a single qualifying word.
Track reuse. If an option can repeat, keep it live even after you've used it once.

blocks.html:
4. Matching Sentence Endings

You get the first half of several sentences and a longer list of possible endings; you choose the ending that completes each one correctly. This type quietly tests two things at once — grammar and meaning — and using both is what separates a right answer from a confident wrong one.

First, the grammar: an ending has to fit the beginning grammatically. If the sentence stem ends with "…researchers were surprised that", the ending needs a clause with a subject and verb, which lets you rule out endings that start with an -ing form or a bare noun. Second, the meaning: among the grammatically possible endings, only one is true according to the passage. Narrow by grammar, decide by meaning. The answers here do follow passage order, which helps you locate each one.

blocks.title: There are always spare endings
blocks.html: Matching Sentence Endings and Matching Features both give you more options than gaps. That's deliberate — the leftovers are there to tempt you. Never pick an ending just because it's grammatically neat; it must also match what the passage actually states. A leftover option is not a mistake in the test, it's bait.

The habit that ties all four together

Notice the through-line: in every one of these types, the trap is a word or name you recognise from the passage attached to a claim the passage doesn't make. The fix is the same each time — answer from meaning, then confirm against the exact wording. Read to the end of the relevant sentence before you commit, and treat any option full of absolutes (all, only, never, proved) with suspicion until the text earns it.

Ready to put this to work on full-length texts? Try the Academic practice set or the General Training set, and check the official band descriptors on the IELTS site. Free preparation with practice tests is also available from the British Council and IDP.

faqs.q: Do multiple-choice answers appear in the same order as the passage?
faqs.a: Yes. Multiple choice, sentence completion and most types follow the order of the text, so each answer sits after the previous one. The main exception is Matching Information, where the answers are deliberately out of order.

faqs.q: Can a paragraph or option be used more than once in matching questions?
faqs.a: Often, yes. In Matching Information a paragraph may be used more than once or not at all, and in Matching Features an option can repeat unless the instructions say otherwise. Always read the instruction line before you assume one answer per option.

faqs.q: Why is the correct multiple-choice option worded differently from the passage?
faqs.a: IELTS tests understanding, not word-spotting, so the right option paraphrases the passage while wrong options often reuse its exact words. Decide what the passage means first, then find the option that says the same thing in different words.

faqs.q: Are these question types the same in Academic and General Training?
faqs.a: Yes. Multiple choice and all the matching types appear in both tests using identical rules. Only the reading passages differ — Academic uses longer academic texts, General Training uses everyday and workplace texts.
